vjimc-2009-cat2-01.title: Digit-sum bookkeeping
vjimc-2009-cat2-01.body:
Let $(a_0a_1\dots a_{b-1})_b$ be self-descriptive. Two facts:
- $a_0\ge1$: the leading digit of a $b$-digit number is nonzero.
- $\sum_ia_i=b$, because $a_i$ counts the digits equal to $i$ and there are $b$ digits.

**(b)** Suppose $a_{b-1}\ge1$. Then some digit equals $b-1$, say $a_j=b-1$, so the digit $j$ occurs $b-1$ times. As the digits sum to $b$, the remaining $b-1$ digits sum to $1$: the multiset of digits is $\{b-1,\,1,\,0,\dots,0\}$ with $b-2$ zeros.
- If $j=0$: the number of zeros is $a_0=b-1\ne b-2$. Contradiction.
- If $j\ge1$: the digit $j$ occurs $b-1$ times, but only two digits are nonzero, so $b-1\le2$. For $b=3$ the digits are $2,1,0$, each occurring once, not $b-1=2$ times. For $b=2$ the digits are $1,1$, there are no zeros, but $a_0\ge1$ — contradiction.

Hence $a_{b-1}=0$: the last digit is $0$.

**(a) Bases with self-descriptive numbers.** $b=4$: $1210$ (and $2020$); $b=5$: $21200$. For $b\ge7$ take
$$a_0=b-4,\quad a_1=2,\quad a_2=1,\quad a_{b-4}=1,\quad a_i=0\text{ otherwise}$$
(e.g. $3211000_7$, $42101000_8$). Since $b-4\ge3$, the positions $0,1,2,b-4$ are distinct; the digits are $b-4,2,1,1$ and $b-4$ zeros, so there are $b-4$ zeros, two $1$s, one $2$, one digit $b-4$ and nothing else — exactly as prescribed.

**No self-descriptive numbers for $b=2,3,6$.** By (b), $a_{b-1}=0$.
- $b=2$: digits $(a_0,0)$ with $a_0\ge1$, so $(1,0)$; it contains one $1$ but $a_1=0$.
- $b=3$: $(a_0,a_1,0)$ with $a_0+a_1=3$, $1\le a_0\le2$: $(1,2,0)$ has one $1$, not two; $(2,1,0)$ has one $0$, not two.
- $b=6$: let $z=a_0\ge1$ be the number of zeros. The digits $a_1,\dots,a_5$ contain $5-z$ nonzero digits with sum $6-z=(5-z)+1$. If $z=5$ the digit sum would be $5\ne6$; so $z\le4$ and these $5-z$ digits are all $1$ except one $2$. Thus the digit multiset is $\{z,2,1^{(4-z)},0^{(z)}\}$:
  - $z=1$: four $1$s, so $a_1=4$, but no digit $4$ is present;
  - $z=2$: $\{2,2,1,1,0,0\}$ forces $a_1=a_2=2$ and $a_0=2$, i.e. three $2$s — contradiction;
  - $z=3$: $\{3,2,1,0,0,0\}$ forces $a_1=a_2=a_3=1$, i.e. three $1$s — contradiction;
  - $z=4$: $\{4,2,0,0,0,0\}$ has no $1$, but then $a_2=1$ (one $2$) would be a $1$ — contradiction.

(A computer search for $b\le11$ confirms: none for $b=2,3,6$; exactly $1210,2020$ for $b=4$, $21200$ for $b=5$, and $3211000$, $42101000,\dots$ for $b\ge7$.)

**Answer: (a) $b=2,3,6$.** ∎

vjimc-2009-cat2-02.title: Cauchy–Schwarz
vjimc-2009-cat2-02.body:
For $f\in E$, by the fundamental theorem of calculus and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,
$$1=f(1)-f(0)=\int_0^1\sqrt{1+x^2}\,f'(x)\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\,dx\le\left(\int_0^1(1+x^2)f'(x)^2dx\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+x^2}\right)^{1/2}=\sqrt{J(f)}\cdot\sqrt{\frac\pi4}.$$
Hence $J(f)\ge\frac4\pi$ for every $f\in E$.

Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz suggests $\sqrt{1+x^2}f'$ proportional to $\frac1{\sqrt{1+x^2}}$, i.e. $f'(x)=\frac{\lambda}{1+x^2}$. Take
$$f_0(x)=\frac4\pi\arctan x .$$
It is $C^1$, $f_0(0)=0$, $f_0(1)=\frac4\pi\cdot\frac\pi4=1$, so $f_0\in E$, and
$$J(f_0)=\int_0^1(1+x^2)\frac{16}{\pi^2(1+x^2)^2}dx=\frac{16}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac\pi4=\frac4\pi .$$
So the minimum is attained at $f_0$ (part a) and equals $\frac4\pi$ (part b).

**Answer: $\min J=\dfrac4\pi$.** ∎

vjimc-2009-cat2-02.title: Expand around the minimiser
vjimc-2009-cat2-02.body:
Let $f_0(x)=\frac4\pi\arctan x\in E$, so that $(1+x^2)f_0'(x)=\frac4\pi$ is constant. Any $f\in E$ can be written $f=f_0+h$ with $h\in C^1[0,1]$, $h(0)=h(1)=0$. Then
$$J(f)=J(f_0)+2\int_0^1(1+x^2)f_0'h'\,dx+\int_0^1(1+x^2)h'^2\,dx=J(f_0)+\frac8\pi\big(h(1)-h(0)\big)+\int_0^1(1+x^2)h'^2\,dx .$$
The middle term vanishes, the last is $\ge0$, so $J(f)\ge J(f_0)=\frac{16}{\pi^2}\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\frac4\pi$, with equality only for $h\equiv0$. Thus the minimum exists, is attained only at $f_0$, and equals $\frac4\pi$. ∎

vjimc-2009-cat2-03.title: Bounding the eigenvalues
vjimc-2009-cat2-03.body:
Let $f(x)=p^2x^{p^2}-q^2x^{q^2}-r^2$. The hypothesis says $f(A)=0$, so the minimal polynomial of $A$ divides $f$ and every (complex) eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A$ satisfies $f(\lambda)=0$:
$$p^2\lambda^{p^2}=q^2\lambda^{q^2}+r^2 .$$

**$\lambda\neq0$**, since $f(0)=-r^2\ne0$.

**$|\lambda|\le1$.** Taking absolute values, $p^2|\lambda|^{p^2}\le q^2|\lambda|^{q^2}+r^2$, i.e. $f(|\lambda|)\le0$. But for real $t>1$, using $p^2>q^2$ (so $t^{p^2}>t^{q^2}$) and $p^2=q^2+r^2$,
$$f(t)>p^2t^{q^2}-q^2t^{q^2}-r^2=r^2\big(t^{q^2}-1\big)>0 .$$
Hence $|\lambda|\le1$.

Therefore $|\det A|=\prod|\lambda_k|\in(0,1]$ (product over the eigenvalues with multiplicity). As $A$ has integer entries, $\det A$ is an integer; a nonzero integer of absolute value at most $1$ has $|\det A|=1$. ∎

(The proof does not use that $r$ is odd.)

vjimc-2009-cat2-04.title: Polynomial method
vjimc-2009-cat2-04.body:
If $m=1$, each partition is the single block $S$, and condition (ii) would require $A_j\cap S=\emptyset$ for $j\neq i$, impossible; so $k\le1=\binom{n-1}{0}$. Assume $m\ge2$.

For each $i$, renumber the blocks of the $i$-th partition so that $1\in S_{1,i}$. Define the polynomial in the variables $x_2,\dots,x_n$
$$P_i=\prod_{l=2}^m\Big(\sum_{s\in S_{l,i}}x_s\Big)$$
(the blocks $S_{l,i}$, $l\ge2$, do not contain $1$). Since these blocks are pairwise disjoint, expanding the product gives a sum of monomials $x_{s_2}x_{s_3}\cdots x_{s_m}$ with distinct indices: $P_i$ lies in the space $V$ spanned by the square-free monomials $\prod_{s\in T}x_s$, $T\subseteq\{2,\dots,n\}$, $|T|=m-1$. So $\dim V=\binom{n-1}{m-1}$, and it suffices to show that $P_1,\dots,P_k$ are linearly independent.

For each $j$ let $\chi_j\in\{0,1\}^{\{2,\dots,n\}}$ be the indicator vector of $A_j\cap\{2,\dots,n\}$. Plugging it in,
$$P_i(\chi_j)=\prod_{l=2}^m\big|A_j\cap S_{l,i}\big| .$$
- For $j=i$, every factor is $1$ by (i), so $P_i(\chi_i)=1$.
- For $j\ne i$, by (ii) $A_j$ misses some block $S_{l_0,i}$. If $l_0\ge2$, a factor is $0$. If only $S_{1,i}$ is missed, then the $m$ elements of $A_j$ lie in the $m-1$ blocks $S_{2,i},\dots,S_{m,i}$, each met at least once, so some block contains $2$ of them and the corresponding factor is $2$. Either way $P_i(\chi_j)$ is even.

Thus the integer matrix $\big(P_i(\chi_j)\big)_{i,j=1}^k$ is congruent to the identity modulo $2$, so its determinant is odd, hence nonzero. If $\sum_ic_iP_i=0$ for real $c_i$, evaluating at each $\chi_j$ gives $\sum_ic_iP_i(\chi_j)=0$ for all $j$, so $c=0$ by invertibility. Hence $P_1,\dots,P_k$ are linearly independent elements of $V$ and
$$k\le\dim V=\binom{n-1}{m-1}. \qquad ∎$$
